title: A&D Precision Limited (Feb 2019 TCC) Tax Court Ruling
subject: Custom Machine Tools: Which Lathe and Grinder Projects Qualify
summary: A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48, is a Tax Court of Canada ruling on SR&ED eligibility for Canadian manufacturers developing custom machine tools. The Court allowed investment tax credits for the welded-steel 80-ton lathe and the abandoned grinder, but denied conventional scaled-down lathes, unallocated 2008 costs, and poorly evidenced repairs to purchased lathes.
metaDescription: Discover the February 2019 Tax Court of Canada decision for A&D Precision Limited regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit eligibility.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Operational Context and the Taxpayer's Claim

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in A&D Precision Limited v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2019 TCC 48 (Docket: 2014-3465(IT)G), delivered by Justice B. Russell on February 28, 2019, represents a seminal judicial authority governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) eligibility within the heavy industrial manufacturing and custom machine-tool engineering sectors. The Appellant, A&D Precision Limited (A&D), is a Canadian privately owned corporation based in Concord, Ontario. Founded in 1974 by its president, sole shareholder, and director, Antranik Derbedrosian—who left school in Syria at age 13 to undertake a five-year machinist apprenticeship before immigrating to Canada in 1969—A&D operates as a sophisticated manufacturer of complex, high-precision metal components utilized in industrial gas turbines and large-scale electrical motors. Throughout the relevant taxation periods, A&D's primary commercial customer, for which A&D has done work over the last 35 years, was General Electric Co. (GE), which constructs massive gas turbines at its Greenville, South Carolina facilities. GE engaged A&D to manufacture components weighing 10,000 lbs to 100,000 lbs (approximately 5 tons to 50 tons) that constantly turn within a gas turbine, requiring great precision, while A&D continuously strove to manufacture these parts as economically as possible in the face of American, Japanese and low-priced Chinese, Brazilian and Mexican competition; the 80 tons (or 100 tons with a steady rest) workpiece capacity referenced later in this report relates to the 80-ton Matteo lathe that A&D designed, not to the GE component range.

To achieve the machining capabilities demanded by GE's evolving turbine specifications, A&D undertook substantial internal capital equipment development and modification initiatives across its fiscal periods ending June 30, 2006, June 30, 2007, and June 30, 2008. In filing its corporate income tax returns and accompanying Form T661 science reports, A&D claimed qualifying SR&ED current expenditures, together with a Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) element pursuant to the regime in force during those taxation years, seeking Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) across four distinct technical projects. Across the three taxation years under appeal, A&D claimed aggregate SR&ED current expenditures of $2,819,325, plus a separate SUE element of $1,333,822, which combined formed the basis for a total of $1,212,213 in disputed federal ITCs.

body.text: Prior to the commencement of the evidentiary hearing before the Tax Court, A&D withdrew two of its four originally submitted SR&ED projects, leaving only Project #4 ("Full spectrum versatile horizontal lathes") and Project #6 ("Double wheel roll grinding machine") for judicial adjudication. Crucially, it was agreed, or in any event decided, in the course of the hearing—at which the Appellant was represented by Adam Gotfried and Justin Kutyan (KPMG Law) and the Respondent by Ifeanyi Nwachukwu and Christopher Kitchen—that only the "science" question was pertinent, and that the "financial" or non-science questions (such as the number of hours claimed and by whom, whether work was undertaken in Canada, or whether the non-scientific elements of SUE had been met) had not been put in issue. Consequently, the sole legal issue before Justice Russell was whether the underlying technical activities executed within Project #4 and Project #6 satisfied the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" pursuant to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (the Act).
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue reassessed A&D for its fiscal periods ending June 30, 2006, 2007, and 2008, denying the claimed ITCs that were placed in issue in the appeal. The judgment does not set out the Minister's assumptions of fact or summarize the Crown's arguments in detail; the only Respondent submission it specifically records is that, if the welded (rather than cast iron) structure of the 80-ton Matteo and the inertia and deflection arising from the unprecedented weight and length of the workpiece gave rise to technological uncertainties, A&D overcame those uncertainties using known solutions. In Canadian tax appeals, as established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Hickman Motors Ltd. v. The Queen, the taxpayer bears the initial legal onus of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact on a balance of probabilities.

Specifically, with respect to Project #4 in the 2006 fiscal period—which related entirely to three commercial heavy-duty Computer Numerical Control (CNC) horizontal lathes acquired from the Italian manufacturer Tacchi Giacomo e Figli SpA (Tacchi), on which A&D, working with Tacchi after the one-year warranty period had expired, attempted to correct problems of undue vibration and backlash—the judgment does not record a specific Crown argument; the Court itself found no basis for the claim. With respect to Project #4 in the 2007 and 2008 fiscal periods—which involved the internal design and assembly of custom horizontal lathes christened the "80-ton Matteo," the "60-ton Matteo," and the "40-ton Matteo"—it was the Court itself, rather than any recorded Crown submission, that observed that the major subsystems identified by A&D (headstock, tailstock, chuck, cutting tool post on the cross slide, carriage on the longitudinal slide, and tailstock sensor control) are usual components of a horizontal lathe, while the Respondent submitted that any uncertainties arising from the 80-ton Matteo's welded structure, inertia and deflection were overcome using known solutions. The judgment likewise does not record the Crown advancing specific arguments about the absence of prototypes or formal test logs; the Court addressed these matters itself in applying the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, noting that testing occurred after assembly rather than on prototypes and that not many records of the testing protocol were made or retained. Finally, regarding Project #6—the design, partial build (in part through refurbishment of an older grinding machine located in Romania) and testing of a novel double-wheel roll grinding machine across the 2006, 2007, and 2008 fiscal periods—the Court itself considered whether a technological advancement could be found when development was ended, after testing revealed excessive vibration, by a business decision based on continuing financial cost, as well as whether the drawings and testimony constituted a sufficient record.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The statutory architecture governing A&D's appeal is anchored in subsection 37(1) and subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, operating in conjunction with the investment tax credit provisions of subsections 127(5) and 127(9). Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), as quoted by the Court, permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature made on SR&ED related to a business of the taxpayer, carried on in Canada and directly undertaken by the taxpayer; the SUE element at issue was addressed by the Court only through the "science" question.

Subsection 248(1) of the Act establishes the exhaustive statutory definition of SR&ED, requiring a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Within the industrial manufacturing context, eligibility turns on paragraph (c) of the definition, which encompasses experimental development—namely, work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Once a base experimental development project is established under paragraph (c), paragraph (d) extends eligibility to commensurate supporting activities, encompassing work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core experimental development.

To operationalize the statutory text of subsection 248(1), Justice Russell relied upon the foundational five-part judicial framework articulated by Justice Bowman (as he then was) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA). Under the first criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the Court evaluates whether there existed a technical risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant scientific or technological field; if the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures, no technological uncertainty exists in law. Under the second criterion, the Court examines whether the person claiming to perform SR&ED formulated specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, following a five-stage process comprising the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

The third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic requires that the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, as well as the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Justice Bowman emphasized that while intuitive creativity and even genius may play a crucial role in the process, and that new technological uncertainties are often identified and resolved as research progresses, those elements must operate within the total discipline of the scientific method. The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advance, that is, an advancement in the general understanding—something known or available to persons knowledgeable in the field; however, the rejection after testing of a hypothesis is nonetheless an advance, and the fact that the initial objective is not achieved invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used, as the very failure may reinforce the measure of the technological uncertainty. Finally, the fifth criterion provides that, although the Income Tax Act and the Regulations do not say so explicitly, it seems self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results be kept, and that it be kept as the work progresses.

In evaluating complex mechanical machinery, Justice Russell also accepted A&D's reliance on the concept of "system uncertainty" as referenced in 1726437 Ontario Inc., o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376, at paragraph 17, where Justice Hogan applied, without particular discussion, paragraph 4.8 of CRA Information Circular IC 86-4R3 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development). Under that paragraph of the Information Circular, work on combining standard technologies, devices and/or processes is eligible if non-trivial combinations of established (well-known) technologies and principles for their integration carry a major element of technological uncertainty, called a "system uncertainty"; Justice Russell also noted that the Respondent's expert, Dr. Yusuf Altintas, acknowledged that system uncertainty could constitute a technological uncertainty, and referred to paragraph 64 of Northwest Hydraulic, where an innovative combination of individually known features was recognized. Furthermore, consistent with Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, once a project is found to be eligible in principle, the specific expenditures and activities must still be vetted against and linked to the eligible technological objectives of the project.
The Court's Final Holding

Following a review of the drawings and other evidence, the oral testimony of Mr. Derbedrosian and of George Predoiu, P.Eng. (who acted as chief engineer on the two projects, other than the Tacchi lathes, as a subcontractor through his personal corporation), the testimony of fact witnesses V. Ouvarov and S. Schiaua, and the evidence of experts Drs. Stephen Veldhuis, Eu-Gene Ng and Yusuf Altintas, Justice Russell allowed the appeal, without costs due to the divided success of the parties, referring the reassessments back to the Minister on a project-by-project and year-by-year basis. For the 2006 fiscal period, the Court disallowed the entirety of the ITCs claimed for Project #4, finding no basis for the claim respecting the three Italian Tacchi lathes because there was little evidence as to what was done and A&D's written submissions made no effort to explain why the Tacchi expenditures would qualify, whereas 100% of the ITCs claimed for Project #6 (the double-wheel roll grinding machine) were allowed as claimed. For the 2007 fiscal period, the Court allowed 100% of the ITCs claimed for both Project #4 (which in 2007 pertained exclusively to the welded-steel 80-ton Matteo lathe) and Project #6. Finally, for the 2008 fiscal period, the Court allowed 100% of the ITCs claimed for Project #6, but allowed only one-third (1/3) of the claimed ITCs for Project #4, disallowing the remaining two-thirds (2/3). Justice Russell determined that while the work on the welded-steel 80-ton Matteo remained eligible SR&ED in 2008, the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteo lathes—built of cast iron, with different off-the-shelf (Timken) spindle bearings and a ball screw instead of a rack and pinion for z-axis movement—involved little originality and differences consistent with conventional design, so that there was no non-trivial system uncertainty; because A&D provided no allocation of its 2008 Project #4 expenditures among the three lathes, the Court allocated one-third of the claim to each lathe.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While A&D Precision is frequently cited as a partial taxpayer victory—representing one of only five successful or partially successful appeals out of sixteen SR&ED judgments rendered by Canadian courts in 2019—the taxpayer suffered substantial financial disallowances across multiple fronts. A&D withdrew two claimed projects prior to the hearing, lost 100% of its Project #4 claim in 2006, and suffered a 66.7% reduction of its Project #4 ITC claim in 2008. Furthermore, the surviving portions of the claim rested substantially on drawings and on the oral testimony of the chief engineer, Mr. Predoiu, who was unwell when he testified and has since passed away, with the Court acknowledging that few records of the testing protocol were made or retained. Dissecting the exact legal, technical, contractual, and accounting deficiencies that triggered the dispute—and contrasting them with the specific evidentiary elements that saved the 80-ton Matteo and Project #6—reveals critical compliance imperatives for Canadian SR&ED practitioners.
Conflation of Vendor Warranty Troubleshooting and Routine Diagnostics with Technological Uncertainty (2006 Project #4: The Three Tacchi Lathes)

The complete disqualification of Project #4 in the 2006 taxation year stemmed from the absence of evidence and argument: the Court found "little evidence as to what was done" on the Tacchi lathes, and A&D's written submissions made no obvious effort to identify that Tacchi expenditures were included in its claim or to explain why they would qualify, stating instead that only the Matteos and the grinding machine were at issue. In or about 2001 and 2002, A&D purchased three large horizontal lathes from Tacchi in Italy—a company considered an international leader in CNC heavy-duty lathes—anticipating that they would enable it to meet GE's more demanding specifications, with the last of the three shipped from Italy in or about March 2004. After installation at A&D's premises, the three Tacchi lathes passed all acceptance tests and tolerance benchmarks, but performance issues soon developed, including headstock vibration, imprecise z-axis carriage movement, and overnight sliding of the tailstock. The one-year warranty period passed, allowing A&D itself, not solely Tacchi, to try to fix or improve the lathes, but without success.

Both A&D and Tacchi engaged Mr. George Predoiu—an Ontario registered professional engineer who trained as a mechanical engineer at the University of Bucharest and had a 47-year career in the design and assembly of machine tools—to provide a neutral view as to the deficiencies of the three Tacchi lathes. Mr. Predoiu was engaged to provide an unbiased view as to the nature and resolvability of the problems. Mr. Predoiu concluded that the three Tacchi lathes were unfixable so as to meet the demandingly tight tolerance requirements of A&D's major customer, GE, and A&D consequently decided to sell them and build its own lathes.

A&D's 2006 Project #4 claim related entirely to the three Tacchi lathes, in respect of which, after the warranty period had expired, A&D working with Tacchi had made attempts to correct or fix the undue vibration and backlash. Justice Russell rejected this claim, stating that he saw no basis for it. The judgment does not analyze the Tacchi work under the Northwest Hydraulic criteria or characterize it as standard diagnostic engineering; the disallowance rested on the lack of evidence and on A&D's failure to explain in its submissions why the Tacchi expenditures qualified. Accordingly, the judgment contains no finding about whether uncertainty regarding why a commercial machine is malfunctioning can constitute a "technological uncertainty"; that remains an analytical inference rather than a holding of the Court. Likewise, the Court did not characterize the joint retention of Mr. Predoiu as evidence of a commercial warranty assessment; it simply recorded that he was retained by both parties as a neutral party. From an evidentiary perspective, Justice Russell observed succinctly that "[t]here is little evidence as to what was done" on the Tacchi lathes. A&D failed to adduce specific hypotheses, experimental modification designs, or structured test data demonstrating an attempt to advance horizontal lathe technology on the Tacchi platforms.
Failure to Demarcate the Boundary Between Systemic Uncertainty and Routine Replication Following Material Substitution (2007 vs. 2008 Project #4: The Matteo Lathes)

The central analytical dichotomy in A&D Precision lies in Justice Russell's contrasting treatment of the 80-ton Matteo lathe (allowed in 2007 and 2008) against the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteo lathes (disallowed in 2008). This demarcation illustrates the exact threshold where "system uncertainty" ends and "routine engineering" resumes under Canadian tax law.

When A&D concluded that the Tacchi lathes should be sold, Mr. Derbedrosian came up with the original concept for a new heavy horizontal lathe designated the "80-ton Matteo," and A&D retained Mr. Predoiu, through his consulting company, as chief engineer for designing and building it; A&D asserted that the 80-ton Matteo was a new machine not available from traditional machine tool suppliers. The concept was a lathe capable of turning an unsupported workpiece weighing 80 tons (or 100 tons with use of a steady rest to support the workpiece) and 13 metres in length, while meeting rigorous tolerance specifications in machining the workpiece. In conventional machine-tool architecture, as A&D acknowledged in its written submissions, most machine manufacturers use cast iron for the main components, as cast iron has density that lessens vibration while steel does not. The judgment does not record A&D's reasons for building the 80-ton Matteo of welded steel rather than cast iron; it notes only that, for the subsequent 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos, A&D had discovered a foundry in China that could do the iron castings.

A&D built the 80-ton Matteo with a welded-steel (rather than cast-iron) structure, assembled largely from parts purchased "off-the-shelf," with Mr. Predoiu making calculations and closely directing and overseeing the assembly; the machine used SKF main spindle bearings and a rack and pinion for movement along the z-axis. Justice Russell found that A&D, with Mr. Predoiu's guidance and expertise, combined known technologies for the manufacture of horizontal lathes with other known technologies pertaining to welded structuring rather than cast iron, and with other technological innovations to address inertia and deflection, made necessary by the intended great size and weight of the workpieces and the aim of machining them with notably extreme accuracy. The judgment does not contain findings on internal damping coefficients, residual weld stresses, thermal distortion, or harmonic resonance; those engineering considerations are not part of the Court's stated reasoning, which focused on inertia and deflection in the context of an 80 ton, 13 metre workpiece. Rather than a Crown argument that lathe components are routine, the Respondent submitted that any uncertainties from the welded structure, inertia and deflection were overcome by A&D using known solutions; Justice Russell—who himself observed that the major subsystems identified by A&D are usual components of a horizontal lathe—nevertheless concluded, considering the evidence as a whole, that A&D faced a technological uncertainty in the form of "system uncertainty," relying on Airmax Technologies (2012 TCC 376) and paragraph 4.8 of IC 86-4R3, Dr. Altintas's acknowledgement, and paragraph 64 of Northwest Hydraulic. Even where individual subsystems are known in the state of the art, the non-trivial combination of those known technologies with welded structuring and innovations addressing inertia and deflection, in the unique context of an 80 ton workpiece and extreme accuracy requirements, amounted to system uncertainty.

However, in the 2008 fiscal period A&D claimed SR&ED for all three Matteo lathes under the same "Project #4" umbrella without any allocation among them, even though it did not assert, as it had for the 80-ton Matteo, that the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos were new machines not available from traditional suppliers. Subsequently to the 80-ton Matteo, A&D built two smaller machines, the 60-ton Matteo and the 40-ton Matteo, which were intended to handle workpieces of up to 60 tons and 40 tons respectively. A&D had discovered a foundry in China that could do the iron castings of the carriage bed, workpiece bed, headstock and tailstock. Consequently, A&D constructed the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos of cast iron rather than welded steel, used a different type of off-the-shelf spindle bearings (Timken rather than SKF, described as "more economical"), and used a ball screw instead of a rack and pinion for movement along the z-axis because that axis was shorter than on the 80-ton Matteo.

Justice Russell held that there was little originality in the design and manufacture of the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos, that each of the three differences A&D highlighted (cast iron, different commercial bearings, and a ball screw drive) was in accord with conventional design, and that the two lathes were in large part simply smaller versions of the 80-ton Matteo, so there was no non-trivial system uncertainty constituting a technological uncertainty. Although additional calculations were required of Mr. Predoiu to help ensure these changes were workable, and the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos were successfully commissioned, the differences were not shown to be so significant as to signify any noteworthy system uncertainty. The use of conventional design features (cast iron, off-the-shelf bearings and a ball screw drive) in scaled-down versions of the 80-ton Matteo resulted in the complete substantive disqualification of the 60-ton and 40-ton lathes.
Accounting and Governance Failure: Unsegregated Cost Pooling Across Eligible and Ineligible Assets (2008 Project #4 Cost Allocation)

A&D compounded its substantive technical error on the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos through a severe project accounting and governance failure in the 2008 taxation year. For its 2008 fiscal period, A&D made a Project #4 claim in respect of each of the three Matteo lathes without any allocation of expenses amongst them; the judgment does not describe A&D's internal ledgers or time-sheet practices.

When the Tax Court determined that only the 80-ton Matteo work in 2008 constituted eligible SR&ED under subsection 248(1), A&D had provided no allocation enabling the Court to determine what proportion of the 2008 Project #4 expenditures was actually incurred on the eligible 80-ton Matteo versus the ineligible 60-ton and 40-ton machines; notably, because the parties had agreed that only the "science" question was in issue, the SUE element of the 80-ton Matteo claim was likewise accepted once that science question was answered in the affirmative. Consistent with the principle in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, even where a project contains eligible SR&ED, specific expenditures must be vetted against and linked to the eligible technological objectives.

Faced with an unallocated claim encompassing three distinct machines—one eligible and two ineligible—Justice Russell, at paragraph 72 of the reasons (with the result confirmed at paragraph 80), allocated one-third of the total SR&ED and SUE expenditures, and thus one-third of the ITCs, claimed for Project #4 for the 2008 fiscal period to each of the three Matteos, allowing the one-third (1/3) share allocated to the 80-ton Matteo and dismissing the two-thirds (2/3) allocated to the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos. This outcome highlights a profound second-order risk for capital-intensive claimants: because the 80-ton Matteo was larger and was the only one of the three found to involve system uncertainty, it may well have consumed a larger share of the 2008 resources than the conventional cast-iron 60-ton and 40-ton builds, although the judgment makes no finding on this point. By failing to provide any allocation, A&D left the Court to apply an equal three-way split, forgoing any opportunity to prove the actual expenditure weighting attributable to the eligible 80-ton Matteo in 2008.
Evidentiary Vulnerabilities: Absence of Formal Test Logs, Non-Production Prototypes, and Commercial Abandonment

Across both Project #4 (the 80-ton Matteo) and Project #6 (the double-wheel roll grinding machine), the Court examined the third, fourth, and fifth criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. The judgment does not record the Respondent specifically arguing that A&D failed to keep laboratory notebooks, failed to build prototypes, or could not show an advancement on the abandoned Project #6; rather, the Court itself noted that testing of the 80-ton Matteo was carried out after assembly rather than on prototypes, that not many records of the testing protocol were made or retained, and that Project #6 was concluded before any successful outcome. While Justice Russell ultimately resolved each of these matters in A&D's favour for the 80-ton Matteo and Project #6, the manner in which A&D succeeded exposes the narrow evidentiary margin on which custom equipment manufacturers operate.

First, regarding contemporaneous documentation, it was acknowledged that not many records pertaining to the carrying out of the testing protocol were made, let alone retained. For the 80-ton Matteo, the evidence included many drawings made under Mr. Predoiu's direction of many significant parts of the machine, but fewer items of evidence exhibiting the engineering calculations he would have carried out; for Project #6, the records were conceptual drawings and drawings of necessary parts. Justice Russell held that these records—in large part drawings—corroborated by the testimony of Mr. Predoiu as chief engineer and Mr. Derbedrosian (A&D's founder and president), whom he found able, knowledgeable and highly experienced, were sufficient, drawing an analogy to ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263, where contemporaneous records combined with oral testimony established that the scientific methodology had been observed. Nevertheless, reliance on oral testimony at trial to link drawings into a coherent narrative of hypothesis testing created immense litigation hazard: as the Court explicitly noted at paragraph 7 of the judgment, Mr. Predoiu was unwell when he testified, and he has since passed away. Had Mr. Predoiu been unable to testify, A&D's documentary record might well have been found insufficient; the 2006 Tacchi claim, on which Mr. Predoiu had no involvement on behalf of A&D, illustrates how a claim fails where there is little evidence as to what was done.

Second, regarding the absence of prototypes, the Court noted that the testing of the 80-ton Matteo was carried out after it had been assembled, as opposed to the creation and testing of prototypes. Justice Russell accepted this approach, reasoning that, given the high cost of this large machine, building any prototype of it would have rendered the total cost of its development prohibitive. When a small or medium-sized enterprise is engineering a 13 metre lathe capable of turning an 80 ton workpiece, it is financially impracticable to construct a disposable, non-production prototype solely for laboratory testing and then scrap it to build a second production unit. Instead, testing of the 80-ton Matteo followed a start-up regimen for new machines, starting and proving one component at a time, and occurred relatively at the end of the building process, which the Court accepted as a consequence of the financial unfeasibility of constructing and utilizing prototypes.

Third, regarding commercial abandonment, in Project #6 A&D sought to develop a novel double-wheel roll grinding machine in which the grinding head could be moved to either side of the middle of the workpiece for grinding, avoiding the need to remove and reposition the workpiece, which could take 16 to 18 hours and risk realignment. A&D knew of no other grinding machine in the world that could do this, Toshiba had quoted $6 million to build such a machine without guaranteeing that it could meet the required tolerances, and the Court found there was no knowledge, within Canada or internationally, of any grinding machine with this design feature, and no reasonable expectation that routine engineering would establish that the design could achieve required grinding tolerances without excessive vibration or "chatter". The machine was built in part from the refurbishment of an older grinding machine located in Romania and was tested, but exhibited excessive vibration; further attempts to minimize vibration (optimizing software to isolate the vibration source, vibration measuring equipment, and a report from a vibration analysis company) were not sufficiently successful, and Mr. Derbedrosian decided A&D would not continue development because of the financial costs that would continue to be incurred. The judgment does not record a specific Crown argument that abandonment precluded technological advancement; Justice Russell addressed the issue himself in considering the fourth criterion. Justice Russell held that the business decision to end the work was the prerogative of a private sector entity, that he would be reluctant to deny SR&ED recognition because the project did not continue to a natural conclusion, and that technological advancement can occur notwithstanding that the work has not proceeded to a natural conclusion, since enough work and testing had been done to ascertain that the machine had not yielded a sufficiently positive result regarding vibration. As stated in Northwest Hydraulic, the fact that the initial objective is not achieved invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used, and, as Justice Russell observed, valuable lessons can be learned from defeat.

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen against the taxpayer's specific factual execution or deficiency across the litigated projects, alongside the legal standard of proof articulated by the Tax Court of Canada.

Tax Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: 1. Existence of Technological Uncertainty (Component vs. Routine Diagnostics)
Income Tax Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. R., 98 DTC 1839 (TCC) (Criterion 1); C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)

Failure (2006 Project #4 - Tacchi Lathes): A&D claimed costs for attempts, made with Tacchi after the warranty period expired, to correct undue vibration and backlash on three purchased Italian CNC lathes, which had exhibited headstock vibration, imprecise z-axis carriage movement, and overnight tailstock sliding. Mr. Predoiu—who had no involvement on behalf of A&D respecting the Tacchi lathes as chief engineer—was retained by both A&D and Tacchi as a neutral party to assess the nature and resolvability of the problems. Execution (Project #6 - Grinder): A&D attempted to design a grinder whose grinding head could be moved to either side of the middle of the workpiece while still achieving fine grinding tolerances without excessive vibration or "chatter".

Standard: Uncertainty must be of a type that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures, i.e., techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Holding: Disallowed for 2006 Tacchi lathes (no basis shown; little evidence as to what was done, and A&D's submissions did not explain why the expenditures qualified). Allowed for Project #6 (no knowledge within Canada or internationally of a grinder with this design feature; technical uncertainty regarding vibration).
2. Systemic Technological Uncertainty ("System Uncertainty" vs. Material Substitution)
Act s. 248(1)(c); 1726437 Ontario Inc. (Airmax Technologies) v. R., 2012 TCC 376; CRA IC 86-4R3, para. 4.8

Execution (2007 & 2008 Project #4 - 80-Ton Matteo): Combining known horizontal lathe technologies with welded structuring (rather than cast iron) and other innovations to address inertia and deflection, to machine an unsupported 80 ton, 13 m workpiece with extreme accuracy, gave rise to system uncertainty. Failure (2008 Project #4 - 60-Ton & 40-Ton Matteos): A&D used conventional cast-iron construction (castings from a Chinese foundry), more economical off-the-shelf Timken spindle bearings, and a ball screw instead of rack and pinion for the shorter z-axis on the smaller lathes.

Standard: System uncertainty exists where non-trivial combinations of established technologies and principles for their integration carry a major element of technological uncertainty. Where a machine is largely a smaller version of an earlier one and its differences accord with conventional design, no non-trivial system uncertainty is shown. Holding: Allowed for 80-ton Matteo. Disallowed for 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos (little originality; largely smaller versions of the 80-ton Matteo with conventional differences).
3. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2)

Failure (2006 Tacchi Lathes): There was little evidence as to what was done, and the Court did not apply the Northwest Hydraulic criteria to the Tacchi work. Execution (80-Ton Matteo & Project #6): Mr. Predoiu, with Mr. Derbedrosian, formulated theories and/or plans (which could be termed hypotheses) to minimize risks due to system uncertainty (80-ton Matteo) and anticipated risks pertaining to vibration (Project #6).

Standard: The claimant must follow a five-stage process: observation of the subject matter of the problem, formulation of a clear objective, identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate it, and methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Holding: Not established for Tacchi lathes; satisfied on 80-ton Matteo and Project #6 based on Mr. Predoiu's testimony.
4. Accordance with the Scientific Method & Prototype Testing
Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3)

Vulnerability / Execution: A&D did not construct prototypes of the 80-ton Matteo; the machine was tested after assembly using a start-up regimen proving one component at a time, and few records of the testing protocol were made or retained. The Project #6 grinder was built in part and tested, with further vibration analysis using optimizing software, vibration measuring equipment and an external vibration analysis report.

Standard: Procedures must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Where building a prototype of a large machine would render the total cost prohibitive, testing after assembly is acceptable; the drawings corroborated testimony that the scientific method was followed. Holding: Satisfied for 80-ton Matteo and Project #6.
5. Achievement of Technological Advancement & Project Abandonment
Act s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4)

Execution (80-Ton Matteo): Creating the new lathe, with system uncertainty arising from modifications to conventional lathe design to handle mammoth workpieces at demanding tolerances, represented a step forward, however incremental, in technical knowledge generally. Vulnerability / Execution (Project #6): Development was ended after testing showed excessive vibration that further attempts did not sufficiently cure, by a business decision based on continuing financial cost to A&D.

Standard: A technological advancement is the gaining of new knowledge that advances general understanding. Advancement can occur even where work has not proceeded to a natural conclusion or been successful, and a business decision to end the work does not disqualify it. Holding: Satisfied for both 80-ton Matteo and abandoned Project #6.
6. Contemporaneous Detailed Records
Act s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5)

Failure (2006 Tacchi Lathes): Little evidence as to what was done on the Tacchi lathes. Execution (80-Ton Matteo & Project #6): Many drawings of significant parts prepared under Mr. Predoiu's direction (with fewer items exhibiting his engineering calculations for the 80-ton Matteo), and conceptual and parts drawings for the grinder, explained via oral testimony.

Standard: A detailed record of hypotheses, tests and results should be kept as the work progresses; its presence is indicative of the scientific methodology. Drawings supplemented by fulsome, credible testimony of those who did the work were sufficient, by analogy to ACSIS EHR, 2015 TCC 263. Holding: Tacchi claim denied for lack of evidence; satisfied for 80-ton Matteo and Project #6.
7. Project-Level Expenditure Segregation & Allocation
Act s. 37(1), s. 127(9); Zeuter Development Corp. v. R., 2006 TCC 597
Failure (2008 Project #4 Cost Pooling): A&D claimed 2008 expenditures for the eligible 80-ton Matteo and the ineligible 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos without any allocation amongst the three.

Standard: Taxpayers bear the burden of tracking and linking claimed expenditures specifically to eligible SR&ED activities. In the absence of any allocation from A&D, the Court allocated the 2008 Project #4 claim equally, one-third to each of the three Matteos. Holding: Two-thirds (2/3) of 2008 Project #4 ITCs disallowed; only one-third (1/3) allowed.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied case studies model realistic Canadian industrial manufacturing scenarios that confront the exact legal, technical, contractual, and accounting pitfalls identified by Justice Russell. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial framework demonstrating how the taxpayer can restructure project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Court's objections and fully satisfy the statutory SR&ED requirements under the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Heavy Aerospace and Energy Turbine Machining — Segregating OEM Defect Troubleshooting from Custom Structural System Uncertainty
Scenario and Inherent A&D Precision Pitfalls

Boreal Turbine Components Inc. ("Boreal"), a precision manufacturer based in Mississauga, Ontario, machines high-nickel superalloy (Inconel 718) casing rings and rotor shafts weighing up to 45,000 kg for civil aviation and power-generation gas turbines. To meet a primary customer's new geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) requirement of ±0.005 mm concentricity across an 8 metre shaft length, Boreal purchases a commercial heavy-duty 5-axis CNC horizontal boring and turning centre from a European manufacturer ("EuroMill GmbH").

Upon installation and commissioning, the EuroMill machine suffers severe regenerative chatter and thermal z-axis drift when machining Inconel 718 at required material removal rates. Boreal spends four months troubleshooting the spindle bearings, servo tuning parameters, and hydraulic counterbalance alongside EuroMill technicians. Eventually, Boreal's lead mechanical engineer determines that the OEM cast-iron column lacks the structural damping and stiffness-to-mass ratio required for continuous 5-axis contouring of large Inconel forgings. Boreal decides to design and fabricate a custom, retrofit gantry-and-bed structural assembly utilizing a novel steel-plate weldment internally honeycombed and injected with an experimental epoxy-granite polymer matrix, coupled with an active piezoelectric tool-post damping system. Because building a disposable 45 ton test rig is financially impossible, Boreal builds and tests the custom assembly directly on its shop floor for commercial production.

If Boreal aggregates all activities from initial EuroMill commissioning through final production into a single SR&ED project, relies solely on final assembly CAD drawings, and cannot produce evidence of what was actually done on the EuroMill machine during the troubleshooting phase, it risks a disallowance comparable to A&D's 2006 Tacchi lathe claim—which failed because there was little evidence as to what was done and A&D did not explain why the expenditures qualified—and may face audit resistance regarding commercial plant construction.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Phase-Gate Boundary Definition

To satisfy the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and avoid the 2006 Tacchi lathe pitfall, Boreal must establish a strict, documented governance firewall separating Phase I (OEM Commissioning, Defect Diagnosis, and Capability Assessment—Ineligible) from Phase II (Experimental Development of the Hybrid Welded-Steel/Epoxy-Granite Damping Structure—Eligible SR&ED). All labour, engineering analysis, and machine downtime incurred during the initial four months of inspecting and adjusting the EuroMill GmbH machine must be classified internally as routine quality assurance, vendor warranty diagnostics, and baseline capability establishment, and excluded entirely from Form T661.

The eligible SR&ED project under paragraph 248(1)(c) may only commence after Boreal's chief professional engineer issues a formal "Technical Capability Exhaustion Report". Mirroring Mr. Predoiu's diagnostic conclusion on the Tacchi lathes, this report must establish through metrological data and kinematic calculations that the OEM equipment cannot achieve the required ±0.005 mm tolerance using standard mechanical adjustments or OEM-recommended modifications, thereby proving that routine engineering solutions have been exhausted. Immediately following this report, Boreal must issue an SR&ED Project Initiation Charter explicitly defining the macro-level "system uncertainty" pursuant to paragraph 4.8 of IC 86-4R3 and Airmax Technologies (2012 TCC 376). The charter must articulate the technological uncertainty not as a commercial goal ("making the machine meet customer tolerances"), but rather as a fundamental gap in mechanical engineering knowledge: specifically, whether a thinner-walled welded-steel structure filled with a non-homogeneous epoxy-granite matrix can achieve a dynamic stiffness exceeding kd ≥ 850 N/µm and a damping ratio of ζ ≥ 0.045 across frequency bands of 40 Hz to 400 Hz without inducing bimetallic-style thermal bowing across an 8 metre axial span due to the divergent coefficients of thermal expansion between welded structural steel (αsteel ≈ 11.5 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and the polymer composite core (αpolymer ≈ 28 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹).
Step 2: Contractual and Vendor Warranty Structuring

In A&D Precision, A&D and the vendor (Tacchi) jointly retained Mr. Predoiu to provide a neutral view on the nature and resolvability of the machine deficiencies, after the one-year warranty period had expired; the Court recorded this fact but did not rely on it in disallowing the 2006 claim, which failed for lack of evidence as to what was done and lack of any explanation of why the expenditures qualified. To eliminate this contractual taint and prevent any reduction of qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18) of the Act for a contract payment (as defined in subsection 127(9)) or other assistance or reimbursement, Boreal must execute a formal commercial settlement or warranty close-out memorandum with EuroMill GmbH prior to commencing Phase II SR&ED. This legal instrument must record that OEM warranty troubleshooting has permanently concluded, stipulate that Boreal assumes 100% of the technical and financial risk for all subsequent structural redesigns, and confirm that EuroMill is providing no financial reimbursement, credit note tied to R&D services, or engineering direction for the custom redesign. Furthermore, when engaging external professional engineering specialists (analogous to Mr. Predoiu), the consulting retainer must be executed solely by Boreal. The Statement of Work must bifurcate initial diagnostic inspection billings (coded to non-SR&ED operational accounts) from subsequent experimental design, finite element analysis (FEA), and harmonic testing billings (coded to SR&ED sub-ledgers), while vesting exclusive ownership of all resulting intellectual property in Boreal.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Architecture

To avoid A&D's perilous reliance on trial-stage oral testimony from an unwell engineer to explain raw blueprints and mathematical calculations, Boreal must embed contemporaneous scientific narrative directly into its engineering workflow as the work progresses. Every CAD drawing revision (such as sequential iterations of the welded internal rib geometry) must contain a mandatory "Hypothesis & Engineering Rationale Block" embedded within the blueprint title sheet. Rather than merely displaying updated geometric dimensions, the revision table must explicitly cross-reference the underlying FEA simulation file and state the specific hypothesis being tested under the five-stage Northwest Hydraulic methodology—for instance, testing the hypothesis that asymmetrical diagonal steel baffling at 35° intervals reduces torsional mode shape amplitude at 125 Hz while preventing epoxy-granite core delamination under thermal cycling from 20°C to 55°C.

Additionally, because Boreal cannot construct a disposable non-production prototype of a 45 ton machine tool, it must document experimental testing on the shop-floor unit using structured metrological test protocols. During sub-assembly integration and trial machining, engineers must preserve dated laser interferometry measurements, accelerometer waterfall plots (Fast Fourier Transform vibration spectra), and thermal imaging gradients mapped directly against predicted mathematical calculations, explicitly recording failed iterations where initial polymer curing shrinkage distorted the linear guideways and necessitated weldment stress-relief modifications.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Segregation on Custom Commercial Assets

Although capital expenditures made after 2013 ceased to qualify for SR&ED incentives, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026) amended section 37 of the Act to restore their eligibility for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Because the retrofitted machine is a permanent shop-floor asset intended for commercial production rather than for use all or substantially all in SR&ED, Boreal cannot claim its capital cost, making accurate segregation between capital fabrication and eligible current SR&ED engineering, analysis, and testing labour under paragraph 248(1)(d) paramount. Boreal must implement weekly digital timecards requiring engineers and machinists to log hours against specific experimental hypothesis codes (differentiating mathematical modelling, FEA analysis, and accelerometer modal testing from routine commercial assembly). Similarly, materials permanently incorporated into the commercial lathe bed must be capitalized to Property, Plant, and Equipment (PP&E), whereas materials consumed or transformed during experimental testing—such as test coupons of epoxy-granite destroyed in compression testing, scrapped trial damping flexures, and sacrificial Inconel test billets machined solely to measure harmonic chatter thresholds—must be tracked on separate SR&ED material requisitions.
Case Study 2: Multi-Unit Custom Industrial Roll-Grinding and Forming Systems — Managing Material Substitution, Scaling Down, and Granular Sub-Project Cost Segregation
Scenario and Inherent A&D Precision Pitfalls

St. Lawrence Heavy Roll Systems Ltd. ("St. Lawrence"), an industrial equipment designer and manufacturer located in Hamilton, Ontario, undertakes a multi-year internal equipment development initiative across two fiscal years to design and build three custom CNC roll-grinding and surface-texturing machines (designated Models RG-100, RG-60, and RG-40) alongside an experimental dual-opposing movable grinding head subsystem (Model DWH-X).

In Year 1, St. Lawrence begins designing Model RG-100 (engineered to grind 100 ton, 15 metre steel mill work rolls) and the Model DWH-X movable dual-wheelhead assembly, which is intended to index across the roll axis so opposing geometries can be ground without unmounting the workpiece. Because no North American foundry can cast a monolithic base for the RG-100 within budget, St. Lawrence engineers a segmented, tension-rod-preloaded welded tubular steel frame for the RG-100. In Year 2, while continuing experimental deflection testing and wheelhead harmonic damping trials on the RG-100 and the DWH-X subsystem, St. Lawrence also fabricates two scaled-down machines—the RG-60 (60 ton capacity) and RG-40 (40 ton capacity)—using conventional cast-iron bases imported from an overseas foundry and standard commercial hydrostatic ways. Midway through Year 2, due to a spike in alloy steel prices and working capital constraints, St. Lawrence's president permanently cancels the DWH-X movable dual-wheelhead project prior to final assembly. In preparing its Year 2 Form T661 claim, St. Lawrence groups the RG-100, RG-60, and RG-40 into a single SR&ED project without segregating labour or subcontractor costs among the three units, and hesitates to claim the cancelled DWH-X work for fear that commercial abandonment precludes SR&ED eligibility.

This scenario replicates the factual pattern of A&D Precision in 2008: claiming an eligible welded-steel machine (the 80-ton Matteo) together with two ineligible cast-iron machines (the 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos) without any allocation—which resulted in an equal one-third allocation and a two-thirds disallowance—alongside a double-wheel grinding project (Project #6) whose development was ended for cost reasons but which the Court nonetheless held to be SR&ED.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Sub-Project Technological Filtering

St. Lawrence must institute a mandatory "Material and Architectural Change Audit" at the outset of Year 2 to prevent routine scaling-down activities from contaminating its eligible SR&ED claim. Whenever an engineering team substitutes a conventional material (imported cast iron on the RG-60 and RG-40) for an experimental material architecture (the tension-preloaded welded tubular steel frame on the RG-100), tax and technical advisors must conduct an immediate reassessment under the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. Because cast iron possesses well-characterized damping and stiffness properties and standard hydrostatic ways follow predictable fluid-film equations, scaling down the machine design to 60 tons and 40 tons represents routine mechanical engineering. Consequently, St. Lawrence must proactively exclude the RG-60 and RG-40 design and fabrication activities from its Year 2 Form T661 claim from inception, restricting its Project #1 claim strictly to the continuing systemic uncertainties of the welded-steel RG-100, and filing Project #2 separately for the DWH-X movable dual-wheelhead architecture.

Simultaneously, when management decides to cancel the DWH-X project in Year 2 due to financial constraints, the chief engineer and chief financial officer must co-sign a formal "Project Suspension and Technical Close-Out Memorandum". This governance record must clearly distinguish the commercial reason for termination (working capital preservation) from the technical status of the investigation at the date of stoppage. Specifically, it must document the technological knowledge gained up to the date of cancellation—such as proving through kinematic modelling and initial test-rig vibration trials that standard curvic couplings could not maintain sub-micron angular repeatability when indexing a 4 ton wheelhead across the work axis without inducing harmonic chatter—thereby cementing eligibility under the fourth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and Justice Russell's holding on Project #6.
Step 2: Contractual and Subcontractor Structuring

When St. Lawrence procures the imported cast-iron bases for the RG-60 and RG-40 and contracts Canadian machine shops to stress-relieve and precision-machine the welded tubular segments for the RG-100, it must enforce strict contractual separation. St. Lawrence must issue distinct Purchase Orders and technical Statements of Work for the RG-100 experimental components versus the RG-60 and RG-40 commercial components, ensuring that vendor invoices never commingle experimental weldment heat-treatment trials with standard cast-iron machining. For Canadian subcontractors performing commensurate supporting work under paragraph 248(1)(d) on the RG-100 or DWH-X—such as third-party modal analysis specialists or custom actuator fabricators—the contracts must explicitly state that the work is performed on behalf of St. Lawrence in Canada, specify the exact technical parameters and testing tolerances required to support St. Lawrence's systemic hypotheses, and itemize engineering and testing services separately from commercial capital deliverables.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Architecture

To ensure that both the continuing RG-100 project and the cancelled DWH-X project satisfy the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic without relying solely on witness memory at trial, St. Lawrence must structure its engineering records around systemic interactions. To substantiate "system uncertainty" under Airmax Technologies and IC 86-4R3 paragraph 4.8, St. Lawrence's engineers must maintain a dated "Sub-System Coupling and Deflection Matrix" for the RG-100. This technical record tracks how variations in one subsystem (such as increasing tension-rod preload from 1,200 kN to 1,800 kN in the welded-steel bed) unpredictably alter the dynamic response of coupled subsystems (such as inducing localized micro-buckling in the guideway mounting pads and shifting the natural resonant frequency of the tailstock spindle into the operating grinding-wheel rotational frequency band). Upon cancelling the DWH-X project, all mathematical calculations, kinematic simulations, dynamic chatter models, and partial sub-assembly test results must be compiled into a date-stamped SR&ED Technical Archive Binder, with each engineering calculation sheet signed by the preparing professional engineer and accompanied by an executive summary translating the mathematical equations into the five-stage hypothesis-testing framework endorsed by the Tax Court.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Financial Cost Segregation

To prevent the two-thirds judicial disallowance imposed in A&D Precision—where Justice Russell allowed only one-third (1/3) of the 2008 Project #4 ITCs because costs for the 80-ton, 60-ton, and 40-ton Matteos were claimed without any allocation—St. Lawrence must implement strict Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) cost-accounting segregation across all work orders:

headers: Ineligible Commercial Account (Models RG-60 & RG-40 Cast-Iron Builds)
Eligible SR&ED Account 1 (Model RG-100 Welded-Steel System Uncertainty)
Eligible SR&ED Account 2 (Model DWH-X Movable Dual-Wheelhead - Abandoned)

cells: ERP Work Order / Job Code
WO-200-COMM-RG60 & WO-200-COMM-RG40 (Excluded from Form T661)
SR-100-EXP-WELD (Claimed on Form T661, Project #1)
SR-300-EXP-DWHX (Claimed on Form T661, Project #2)
Engineering Labour (P.Eng. & Designers)
Standard CAD drafting, bill of materials generation, and commercial component sizing for cast-iron beds.
Mathematical deflection modelling, FEA stress analysis, and iterative redesign of tensioned welded-steel bed.
Kinematic indexing calculations, harmonic chatter modelling, and structural design up to cancellation date.
Shop-Floor Machinist & Assembly Labour
Routine machining, scraping of cast-iron ways, ball-screw installation, and standard alignment.
Directly supporting experimental trials: installing strain gauges, laser alignment verification under 100 ton test loads, and structural rework.
Fabrication and bench-testing of experimental wheelhead indexing mechanism prior to project termination.
Materials Consumed / Transformed
Capitalized inventory or Cost of Goods Sold (100% excluded from Form T661).
Sacrificial test plates, strain gauges, and weld coupons destroyed during destructive and non-destructive deflection testing.
Custom-machined prototype indexing couplings and test fixtures scrapped upon project cancellation.

body.text: By segregating every hour of engineering and shop-floor labour through digital job-card scanning tied directly to SR-100-EXP-WELD and SR-300-EXP-DWHX, and isolating all routine work on the cast-iron RG-60 and RG-40 units into WO-200-COMM, St. Lawrence establishes a verifiable financial audit trail. Even when a CRA Research and Technology Advisor and Financial Reviewer audit the facility simultaneously constructing all three machines, St. Lawrence can substantiate to the dollar that 100% of the claimed expenditures relate exclusively to the welded-steel RG-100 systemic uncertainty and the novel DWH-X movable wheelhead investigation, completely insulating the claim from judicial estimation reductions.
Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in A&D Precision Limited v. Her Majesty The Queen (2019 TCC 48) provides an authoritative analytical framework for navigating the intersection of heavy mechanical engineering and Canadian SR&ED tax law. First, the judgment confirms that custom capital equipment manufacturers can successfully invoke the "system uncertainty" concept reflected in Airmax Technologies and CRA Information Circular IC 86-4R3 paragraph 4.8 where known technologies are combined with unconventional structural approaches—such as welded steel in place of the conventional cast iron—and other innovations to address inertia and deflection under unprecedented load and precision demands, even when individual mechanical components are usual in isolation. Second, the Court demonstrated strong commercial realism regarding the third, fourth, and fifth criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, holding that the 80-ton Matteo did not require a prototype whose cost would have been prohibitive, that drawings corroborated by fulsome, credible testimony of those who did the work could satisfy the record-keeping criterion despite limited testing records, and that a business decision to end development because of continuing financial cost does not strip systematic experimental work of its SR&ED eligibility.

Conversely, the taxpayer's partial disqualifications within the same judgment establish bright-line compliance boundaries. The 2006 Tacchi lathe claim—relating to attempts to fix purchased commercial machinery—failed because there was little evidence as to what was done and A&D offered no explanation of why the expenditures qualified; claimants pursuing similar work must be prepared to prove, with evidence, what was done and why it constitutes SR&ED. Furthermore, where later machines are largely smaller versions of an eligible machine and their differences (cast iron, off-the-shelf bearings, ball screw drives) accord with conventional design (the 2008 cast-iron 60-ton and 40-ton Matteos), the Court will not find the non-trivial system uncertainty that qualified the original. Above all, A&D Precision underscores that substantive technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) is inseparable from granular cost accounting under subsection 37(1): commingling eligible experimental assets with routine commercial builds inside an unallocated expenditure pool invites severe judicial discounting, turning what should have been a full recovery on flagship engineering work into a costly, self-inflicted tax forfeiture.
